title: Scheduled Tasks and Weekly Sentiment
summary: Schedule calendar jobs and calculate journal summaries with explicit periods and duplicate handling.

sources.title: Engineering Digest: Ultimate Guide to Scheduling Tasks with Cron Jobs in Spring Boot
Engineering Digest: Adding Sentiment to Journal App

richText: Choose a time rule
@Scheduled runs a Spring bean method automatically. Add @EnableScheduling to a configuration class to activate annotation-based scheduling.
Use fixedDelay for polling that should wait a set time after the previous run finishes. Use fixedRate for a periodic target interval measured between scheduled starts.
Use cron for calendar rules, such as every Sunday morning. Spring cron has six fields: second, minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week.
0 0 9 * * SUN means Sunday at 09:00:00. The zone attribute chooses the timezone. Server timezone settings should not silently change the business schedule.
This example uses Spring Boot 3, Spring Framework 6, and Java 17. The scheduled method has no arguments and delegates work to a service.
Run a weekly digest
WeeklyDigestService is the application service that selects eligible users, calculates summaries, and queues digest events. Keep this work separate from the timing rule.
When the application is running on Sunday at 09:00 in Asia/Kolkata, Spring invokes aggregateAndQueue. An application that is stopped does not execute this annotation.
Calculate a journal sentiment summary
Sentiment is a label for an entry, such as HAPPY, SAD, or ANGRY. The course topic adds this label to the journal application.
For each opted-in user, read entries in one fixed reporting interval. Exclude missing sentiment labels and count each remaining label.
For labels HAPPY, SAD, HAPPY, the counts are HAPPY=2 and SAD=1. The most frequent label is HAPPY.
Define what happens on equal counts. For HAPPY=1 and SAD=1, use a documented tie rule or report both labels. Iteration order should not silently decide the result.
Use the same start and end instants for the entire run. Decide whether “week” means the last seven days or a calendar week in the selected timezone.
An empty interval produces no summary. This aggregation counts stored labels. It does not diagnose a person or prove that an AI model analyzed the entry text.
Handle restarts and multiple instances
Every application instance has its own scheduler. Two running instances can both queue the same digest. A timezone does not prevent this duplication.
Use a durable job record with a unique user-and-reporting-period key, a shared lock, or a dedicated scheduler when only one instance should run the job.
Persist a pending state if work must survive restarts. Plain @Scheduled does not replay a missed Sunday execution by itself.
Bound database batches and network timeouts. Record failed users separately so one unavailable provider does not hide the remaining work.
Queue emails after aggregation. Scheduler completion, Kafka acknowledgment, and email delivery are separate events.
